title: Matrix Aluminum Piping: first-quarter purchases budget with 15% safety stock, plus safety stock and sales budget considerations
participant_role: Controller for Matrix Aluminum Piping, Inc., a wholesale aluminum pipe supplier, preparing the first-quarter purchases budget
judge_role: Purchasing manager for Matrix Aluminum Piping who wants the purchase budget and a discussion of safety stock and sales budgets
scenario:
You are to assume the role of the controller for MATRIX ALUMINUM PIPING, INC., a major wholesale supply company for the aerospace, automobile and railroad industry. The purchasing manager (judge) wants you to prepare a purchase budget, as well as discuss safety stock levels and sales budgets.

You are working on budgeting for purchases for the first quarter of next year. You prepare a budget for each type of pipe, currently focused on the 8 ft 3/4 inch pipe, inventory item #254-11 with an average cost of $15 each.

You sent the assistant controller out to the warehouse to count the number of pipes on hand on December 31, the number of units is 50,000. MATRIX purchases most of the aluminum pipes from northeast Canada. There have been several instances where winter storms have caused an interruption in the supply chain, therefore, you want to increase the safety stock for all pipes to 15% of next month's sales for the estimated ending inventory.

You have met with the sales manager and worked out a sales budget in units for the first quarter. The information is below.

[Budgeted Unit Sales, January through April: see exhibits]

You are to prepare a purchases budget for the first quarter of next year, January, February, and March by completing the table below. Then, you will meet with the purchasing manager (judge) to go over the results.

[Purchases budget table to complete: see exhibits]

The purchasing manager (judge) would like to know:
- How you budgeted the unit purchases
- What is considered when deciding on a safety stock level?
- What is considered when developing the sales budget?

You will present the information to the purchasing manager (judge) in a role-play to take place in the manager's (judge's) office. The purchasing manager (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the manager's (judge's) questions, the purchasing manager (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: How is the first quarter different from other quarters regarding safety stock?

solution.overview: A strong answer builds the purchases budget month by month: budgeted sales plus desired ending inventory (15% of next month's sales) equals units needed, less beginning inventory (50,000 in January, then the prior month's ending inventory) equals budgeted purchases of 417,500, 465,000 and 542,500 units. The presenter then explains the factors behind the safety stock level (supplier location and ratings, historical trends, aluminum shortages) and the sales budget (historical trends, the economy, seasonal demand, aluminum price forecasts), and ties the budget to bottom-up input from the sales manager.

answer: Estimated ending inventory = 15% of next month's sales: Jan 67,500 (15% x 450,000); Feb 82,500 (15% x 550,000); Mar 75,000 (15% x 500,000)
Units needed = sales + ending inventory: Jan 467,500; Feb 532,500; Mar 625,000
Beginning inventory: Jan 50,000 (physical count), Feb 67,500, Mar 82,500 (each month's beginning = prior month's ending)
Budgeted purchases = units needed minus beginning inventory: Jan 417,500; Feb 465,000; Mar 542,500
At $15 average cost the dollar purchases are about $6.26 million, $6.98 million and $8.14 million, or $21.4 million for the quarter

by_task.task: How the unit purchases were budgeted
answer: Started from the sales budget agreed with the sales manager (a bottom-up input)
Added the desired safety stock so we finish each month with 15% of the next month's needs already on the shelf
Subtracted what we already have at the start of the month so we only buy the gap
April's sales figure is needed only to set March's ending inventory
This is a preliminary budget: it will be revised as actual sales and supplier lead times come in

by_task.task: What is considered when deciding on a safety stock level
answer: Historical trends in demand and in stock-outs
Suppliers' ratings: reliability and on-time delivery record
Location of the supplier: northeast Canada means winter storms can interrupt shipments
Aluminum shortages and lead times in the market
The cost trade-off: more safety stock ties up cash (about $15 per pipe) and storage space, too little risks lost sales to aerospace, auto and railroad customers

by_task.task: What is considered when developing the sales budget
answer: Historical sales trends by month and product
The overall economy and the health of the aerospace, automobile and railroad industries
Seasonal demand patterns (for example, the March peak of 550,000 units)
Aluminum price forecasts, since price changes affect how much customers order
Input from the sales team and known customer contracts (bottom-up budgeting)

calculations.label: Estimated ending inventory (15% of next month's sales)
Budgeted purchases in dollars at $15 average cost (model answer, not in PDF)

judge_question_answers.question: How is the first quarter different from other quarters regarding safety stock?
answer: The first quarter is winter, when storms in northeast Canada have repeatedly interrupted our supply chain, so the risk of late shipments is highest
That is why the safety stock is being raised to 15% of next month's sales now; in calmer quarters a lower percentage may be enough
Sales also climb through the quarter (400,000 to 550,000), so each month's safety stock must cover a bigger following month
Safety stock should be reviewed each quarter against actual supplier performance and demand

key_concepts.definition: A schedule of how many units (or dollars) must be bought each period. Budgeted purchases = Budgeted sales + Desired ending inventory minus Beginning inventory.
Extra inventory kept on hand to protect against supply delays or unexpected demand. Here it is set at 15% of the next month's budgeted sales.
The units a company wants on hand at the end of a period, usually a percentage of next period's sales; it becomes the next period's beginning inventory.
The forecast of units and dollars to be sold each period. It is the starting point for the purchases, production and cash budgets.
A formal written plan of expected revenues, costs and resource needs for a future period, used to coordinate departments and control spending.
Budget built from estimates by the people closest to the work (for example, the sales manager's unit forecast) and rolled up to the company level.
Senior management sets overall targets and allocates them down to departments.
Starting from last period's budget or actuals and adjusting up or down by a percentage or for known changes.
Every line item must be justified from zero each period rather than carried forward.
Selecting suppliers, negotiating price and terms, ordering the right quantity at the right time, and monitoring supplier performance and lead times.
The time between placing an order and receiving the goods; longer or less reliable lead times call for more safety stock.
Lost sales, rush shipping and customer goodwill lost when inventory runs out; balanced against the carrying cost of holding extra stock.
